The primary objective of this research is to explore the impact of collision cascade processes on thin layers that have been exposed to irradiation. To achieve this goal, the collision cascade is simulated using the Monte Carlo code SRIM, and the results are compared to those obtained from the Geant4-DNA package. The findings reveal that the SRIM simulation yields a significantly higher critical angle for nanopatterning than the Geant4-DNA package. This discrepancy is attributed to the SRIM package's ability to more accurately model the collision cascade's specifics. Consequently, the SRIM package is recommended for irradiation experiments that rely on the formation of nanoparticles in thin layers.

This paper introduces a novel anti-copy mechanism for C# classes, which leverages a navigation approach to prevent unauthorized access. By making fields and properties inaccessible, the mechanism compels other classes to obtain necessary data through a navigation object, which can be made accessible. Our implementation, which is available in the GitHub repository https://github.com/luizgomes/NavNavAntiCopy, allows for the creation of a custom C# class that enforces this approach.

This paper investigates the complete convergence of automorphic Dirichlet series, specifically examining complete convergence of Dirichlet series linked to Hecke-Maass forms. It also derives an estimate for the Bessel function $J_{\sigma}(y)$, which plays a significant role in this estimation process.

Let G be a group and H a subset, with a given word metric on the group G. H is called a quasi-normal subgroup if it remains unchanged under any group element's action, with only a limited number of errors. We demonstrate that if H satisfies this condition, it must be a normal subgroup within the group. We also show that if H is finitely generated, it must be a finite collection of elements.

Log-concave density estimation is a widely used method for non-parametric density estimation, but its computational complexity is a significant drawback. To overcome this issue, we introduce a new approach that combines a novel algorithm with a more efficient data structure. This algorithm builds upon a previously proposed method, but our data structure significantly reduces the time required to calculate the log-concave density. By employing a divide-and-conquer strategy, we achieve a substantial improvement in computational efficiency, reducing the time required to calculate the log-concave density from O(n^2) to O(n log n). Our results show that this novel approach yields accurate estimates comparable to existing methods, but with a significant reduction in computational time.

We introduce an innovative Monte Carlo approach to study granular matter's entropy by utilizing the Wang-Landau algorithm. This enables the direct calculation of the density of states for configurations in a specific volume range. Our method focuses on configurations with a particular structure, which are common in granular matter. We validate our approach by comparing its results with those from molecular dynamics simulations, which are based on the canonical ensemble.

The classic game of Cops and Robbers is a well-known two-player pursuit game on graph boards, where cops attempt to capture the robber, who tries to evade capture. This paper introduces a new variation of the game, known as the Adventurer-Manager Game, which is a two-player pursuit game on graph boards, where the manager tries to guide the adventurer to victory, while the adventurer attempts to defeat the three adventurers. We investigate the adventurer-manager number of a graph, which represents the minimum number of adventurers required to guarantee the manager's victory.

We've developed a statistical method to identify and link frequency patterns in two time series that may have multiple oscillations. This method is based on analyzing individual time series using the Gaussian process model, which allows us to explore a broad range of possible patterns. We've established a mathematical relationship between the patterns of two time series, which can be represented by a specific function. This function can be used to calculate the strength of the relationship between specific frequency patterns, which we've defined as the frequency-frequency association. We've also developed a statistical method to test for significant associations, which takes into account the patterns of individual time series. We've tested our method using simulated data and real-world examples, including the relationship between two time series from a neuroscience experiment.

This study explores the engagement solutions for a higher-order Broer-Kaup system in (1+1) dimensions through a systematic approach. A new method is used to derive the Lax pair, bilinear form, and (n+2)-component linear system for the higher-order Broer-Kaup system. A new method is proposed to obtain and analyze the engagement solutions of this system, which is then applied to derive and classify various solutions, including solitons, rational, and exponential types. A detailed examination of (n+2)-component linear system solutions reveals a unique class of solutions, which is subsequently used to derive and classify engagement solutions for the higher Broer-Kaup system.

We examine the energy conservation of weak solutions for the incompressible Euler equations, focusing on the condition that for all smooth functions of velocity, the integral of the product of the function and its image under the operator is non-negative. We link this condition to the circulation of the velocity field around closed loops, providing a new criterion for conserving energy in these equations.

The VIRUP virtual reality project is a collaborative effort between the European Southern Observatory and the Max Planck Institute for Radio Astronomy, aiming to create immersive virtual experiences for astronomy enthusiasts. This document outlines the project's objectives and describes its key components, including the Virtual Reality Cosmos tool, which allows users to explore 3D visualizations of astronomical data. VIRUP also provides access to other relevant virtual reality applications and sets forth its goals and future plans.

The vast and rapidly expanding universe is a captivating topic for children, 
offering a unique chance to explore data in a tangible way. We introduce the 
Data Bricks Cosmic Expedition, a project that utilizes physical data 
representation to educate kids about data. Through this project, we investigate 
the effectiveness of this approach in making data accessible and engaging for 
children.

Modern data-plane software, such as OpenFlow, is highly complex, comprising numerous functions that serve various purposes. These functions, however, are not always utilized, and some may even be detrimental to system performance. To address this issue, we propose a novel approach to identify the active functions within a data-plane, specifically in the context of Software Defined Networking. Our method, referred to as FuncPath, relies on analyzing the execution paths of these functions, and it successfully pinpoints the most frequently accessed paths, which we term functional data-paths. These paths, however, are not always reflective of the entire data-plane, and so we also identify the inactive components that are not part of any path. To validate the effectiveness of FuncPath, we applied it to three real-world OpenFlow switches, and the results demonstrate that it can identify up to 90% of the active functions, and up to 95% of the inactive components, with a high degree of accuracy.

A significant challenge in computer vision is disentangling data representations, which is crucial for tasks like data augmentation and transfer learning. To address this, researchers have developed methods that utilize prior knowledge to guide representation learning. However, this approach is limited by the need for extensive prior knowledge. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a novel approach that leverages relational intelligence to learn weakly disentangled data representations without relying on prior knowledge. Our method utilizes a relational neural network to model relationships between data samples and their corresponding latent representations, which is then used to guide the learning process. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on a variety of image datasets, including the CelebA, Office-Home, and CUB datasets, and show that it outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in terms of both disentanglement and generalization.

The potential for generating renewable energy from ocean waves has driven research into the use of flexible foils in wave energy systems. This study investigates the interaction between the wake of a front foil and a back foil in a tandem configuration, where both foils are capable of heaving and pitching. Through experiments in a wave tank, researchers examined how the back foil's motion is influenced by the front foil's movements and how this relationship affects the overall energy collection efficiency of the system. The study found that the back foil's motion is closely linked to the front foil's motion, with a phase difference that depends on the wave frequency. This phase difference can be used to optimize the performance of the tandem system, with the most efficient configurations occurring when the phase difference is around 180 degrees. The study also revealed that the wake of the front foil can be used to enhance the performance of the back foil, with the most efficient configurations occurring when the phase difference is around 180 degrees.

To estimate real-time dynamics from lattice QCD, we employ Bayesian inverse methods. The proposed approach is applied to a simplified model of quantum dynamics in a potential, demonstrating the capability to reconstruct the underlying potential and its associated spectral properties. The effectiveness of this method is further assessed by applying it to a theoretical QCD scenario involving the temporal correlation of a pseudoscalar bilocal operator. The resulting estimates of the spectral function and the Polyakov loop are compared against their known analytical counterparts.

The interaction between a quantum dot and a superconductor is crucial for creating hybrid devices that can host Majorana modes. This research investigates the charge transfer between a quantum dot and a superconducting electrode by analyzing the sensitivity of the dot's energy levels to adjacent gates. This analysis reveals that the dot's energy levels are influenced by the occupation of the dot and a nearby gate, with the effect being more pronounced at higher gate voltages. This finding suggests that the dot and gate are connected through a weakly coupled quantum state, with the electron transfer between them being mediated by a tunneling process. This research provides a deeper understanding of the charge transfer between a quantum dot and a superconducting electrode, which is essential for designing and fabricating Majorana-based quantum devices.

The process of designing novel compounds with targeted properties is a complex task that requires a deep understanding of molecular structures and their effects on desired outcomes. In this study, we present a novel energy-driven generative model that combines the strengths of variational autoencoders and Boltzmann machines to tackle this challenge. Our model incorporates a molecular encoder that maps molecules to a latent space, where the likelihood of a given molecule being generated is inversely proportional to its energy. By utilizing a hybrid loss function that combines variational and energy-based learning techniques, we achieve a balance between generating high-quality molecules and ensuring their diversity. Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach in producing molecules with targeted properties, including those with high binding affinity to a specific protein.

We propose a new type of graph called the Interaction Machine, which is a
directed graph that uses tokens to represent dynamic interactions. Our work
includes a comprehensive study of the token-based graph's topology, including
its properties, subgraphs, and a unique decomposition method. We also develop
algorithms for token manipulation and graph analysis, and demonstrate the
efficiency of our methods through a series of experiments. Our results show that
the Interaction Machine provides a flexible and expressive framework for
modeling complex systems, and we believe it has the potential to be applied in
a wide range of fields, including system design, data analysis, and network
modeling.

The Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC) is experiencing a significant outward movement, which is crucial for understanding the dynamics of the Local Group. Researchers have employed a unique method to measure the motion of the LMC by analyzing the proper motions of its member stars. The study utilized data from the VMC survey to identify and analyze the motion of the LMC, taking into account the influence of the Small Magellanic Cloud (SMC). The results show that the outer regions of the LMC are moving at a significantly higher velocity than the inner regions, which is consistent with the hypothesis that the SMC is responsible for this motion. The study also found that the motion of the LMC is consistent with the predictions of the tidal tail hypothesis, which suggests that the motion of the LMC is caused by the interaction between the LMC and the SMC. The study provides new insights into the motion of the LMC and the dynamics of the Local Group, and it has important implications for our understanding of the evolution of the LMC and the SMC.

The widespread adoption of Advanced Metering Infrastructure (AMI) has significantly improved the efficiency of smart grid operations, enabling utilities to collect and analyze real-time smart meter data. This data can be used to identify energy theft by analyzing abnormal patterns in smart meter readings. A novel approach to detecting energy theft is presented, which utilizes a deep recurrent neural network to analyze smart meter data. The proposed method employs a hybrid loss function that combines binary cross-entropy and mean square error loss functions to enhance the network's performance. The proposed network is further enhanced with a dynamic hyper-parameter adjustment mechanism, which adjusts the learning rate and dropout rate during training to improve detection accuracy. The proposed method is evaluated using real-world data from a UK smart grid, and the results demonstrate its effectiveness in detecting energy theft with high accuracy.

We employ a novel method to construct tight surface graphs through inductive surface transformations, which yield not only the exact edge count but also provide a geometric understanding of these graphs.

Using data from 0.3 inverse femtobarns of proton-proton collisions at 7 and 8 TeV, we analyzed the lifetimes of promptly formed $\Omega^{0}_{c}$ and $\Xi^{0}_{c}$ baryons. These lifetimes were determined by reconstructing their decay products and measuring their transverse momentum. The results showed that the lifetimes of $\Omega^{0}_{c}$ and $\Xi^{0}_{c}$ baryons are 144 and 1.45 times those of $\Omega^{0}$ and $\Xi^{0}$, respectively. These findings are consistent with predictions from the heavy quark expansion theory.

Unsupervised hyperspectral image classification (HSI) has been a significant focus in the field of remote sensing research. Traditional methods, such as subspace clustering, have been widely used for this task. However, existing subspace clustering methods often overlook the importance of the similarity between spectral pixels and ground truth classes. To address this issue, a new framework called Similarity-constrained Subspace Clustering (SSC) has been proposed. SSC incorporates a similarity-constrained matrix to link the subspace clustering process with the similarity between spectral pixels and ground truth classes. By jointly optimizing the graph structure, the similarity-constrained matrix, and the subspace representation, SSC can effectively improve the classification performance. Furthermore, a fast algorithm has been developed to efficiently solve the SSC framework. Experimental results on three real-world hyperspectral datasets demonstrate that SSC outperforms state-of-the-art unsupervised HSI classification methods.

A novel model of snow dunes on Arctic sea ice has been developed to simulate the formation of dunes in undisturbed snow cover. This model, which uses a combination of mathematical equations, incorporates the effect of gravity on the snow cover's surface. By applying this model to Arctic conditions, researchers have found that the formation of dunes is influenced by factors such as the size of ice ridges and the amount of solar radiation. This model, which can be applied to other types of snow cover, provides insight into the complex interactions between snow, ice, and the environment.

A theoretical study of dynamic magnetic field interactions on ultracold atom-molecule processes reveals a phenomenon known as the selective quantum Zeno effect. The application of a dynamic magnetic field can effectively suppress the spontaneous emission of an atom-molecule system, thereby inhibiting its transition to other states. The findings demonstrate that an uncontrolled dynamic magnetic field can effectively prevent the dissociation of molecules into individual atoms, while an uncontrolled static magnetic field can effectively prevent the formation of molecules from atoms. The research has significant implications for the development of novel dynamic control methods for ultracold atom-molecule interactions.

A nonextensive version of Itô-Langevin mechanics is developed, where the Itô equation is modified by incorporating Tsallis statistics, and the resulting kinetic equation is derived. This kinetic equation exhibits characteristics of non-Maxwellian distributions, and it is shown that the system converges to a nonextensive equilibrium state. Furthermore, the system's relaxation dynamics is analyzed, and the resulting distribution is found to be consistent with the Tsallis one. Additionally, the system's transport properties are investigated, and the resulting viscosity and thermal conductivity are calculated.

In recent years, research has focused on the study of topological semimetals, which exhibit unique properties such as Dirac points, nodal lines, and Weyl points. These properties can be manipulated through external stimuli, such as electric fields, magnetic fields, and strain. This study explores the creation of Weyl points with higher-order topology in a specific type of material, an optimally stimulated non-hermitian nodal-line semimetal. By introducing a type of non-hermitian perturbation, we demonstrate that the original nodal lines are transformed into Weyl points, which exhibit unique properties such as Fermi arcs and Fermi strings. These properties can be further enhanced by introducing a type of non-hermitian skin effect, which results in the emergence of Fermi strings. This study provides a theoretical framework for understanding the behavior of Weyl points in topological semimetals, and has potential applications in the development of novel electronic devices.

A novel blockchain protocol called Marvel DC has been developed to efficiently handle distributed computing tasks. It achieves this by utilizing a two-stage process where the master node first assigns tasks to workers and then verifies their results. To prevent malicious behavior, the protocol incorporates a reward system that incentivizes workers to provide accurate results. Furthermore, the protocol's design allows it to function without a central authority, thereby ensuring decentralization. Experimental results demonstrate the protocol's effectiveness in terms of performance and security.

A new model for assessing the quality of 3D point cloud compression is introduced. This model, called the Decreased Reference Perceptual Quality Model (DR-PQM), is designed to be computationally efficient and is based on a reduced set of reference data. This model is an extension of the Rate Perceptual Quality Model (RPQM), which is enhanced by incorporating a more accurate representation of point cloud geometry. This improved representation is made possible by utilizing a subset of the point cloud as reference data, which is then used to improve the quality of the reconstructed point cloud. This new model is evaluated on a set of publicly available point cloud sequences and is shown to be effective in predicting point cloud quality.

We investigate the QCD phase diagram in a strong magnetic field using the AdS/CFT correspondence, focusing on the behavior of a holographic model that incorporates a chiral phase transition and melting of the color superconductor phase. Our study examines the relationship between the model's parameters and the QCD thermodynamic properties, particularly the order parameter and free energy density. We found that the model's behavior aligns with mean-field theory and that the relationship between the model's parameters and QCD thermodynamic properties can be used to constrain the model's parameters. Furthermore, we found that the model's behavior can be used to distinguish between different types of color superconductors, such as the color superconductor phase and the chiral phase transition phase. Our study also highlights the importance of the model's behavior in understanding the QCD thermodynamic properties, particularly the behavior of the model's parameters in the presence of a strong magnetic field.

Recent advancements in deep learning have led to a surge in interest in self-supervised learning (SSL), which has shown promising results in medical imaging. However, the majority of SSL methods are designed for 2D images, and their application to 3D images is hindered by the high computational costs. This study presents a novel approach called slice-driven SSL (SB-SSL) that leverages the strengths of pre-trained transformers and SSL to address knee anomaly classification from 3D MRI scans. The proposed method involves two key components: a slice-by-slice 2D transformer that extracts features from individual slices, and a slice-to-volume SSL module that learns from the interdependencies between adjacent slices. The SSL module is trained using a contrastive learning approach, and the final classification is performed using a 2D transformer-based decoder. Experimental results on the OAI dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method, with a significant improvement in the AUC metric compared to existing state-of-the-art methods.

The widespread use of digital devices has led to a growing interest in creating novel, personalized, and unique text styles. However, the development of new typefaces is a labor-intensive process that requires extensive knowledge and expertise. To address this challenge, we introduce a new approach that enables the creation of new typefaces from limited examples. Our method involves a multi-stage process that first generates a basic font structure and then refines it to capture the specific style of the target typeface. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method through a comprehensive evaluation on a large dataset of text images, showing that it can successfully create new typefaces with as few as two examples.

We investigate the torsional effects on a liquid in equilibrium, considering its density and chiral properties. The liquid's free energy is expressed as a function of density and a measure of chirality, allowing us to derive the pressure and chemical potential. The pressure is found to have a dependence on chirality, leading to an additional torsional force per unit area, which is influenced by the liquid's density and a specific coefficient. The chemical potential is similarly affected, resulting in an additional energy contribution. The equilibrium condition is established by minimizing the free energy, leading to a relationship between the torsional force, density, and chirality coefficient, which is further constrained by the conservation of angular momentum.

The dynamic nature of adaptive video streaming has led to the development of various QoE enhancement schemes. These schemes typically adjust the quality of the next video segment based on the user's past experience. However, this approach has limitations, as it relies on a limited number of historical data points and may not accurately capture the user's preferences. To address this issue, we propose a new method that utilizes a digital twin of the user to predict their QoE based on a comprehensive set of user data. This prediction enables the streaming system to optimize the quality of subsequent video segments, thereby enhancing the user's overall experience. The proposed method is evaluated using a real-world dataset and demonstrates significant improvements in QoE compared to existing approaches.

The KM3NeT/ARCA, a high-energy neutrino telescope, is being constructed in the Mediterranean Sea and utilizes a vast array of photomultiplier tubes to detect the Cherenkov light produced by muons. This light is scattered within the water, leading to a phenomenon known as the'scattering tail' that can distort the muon track. Consequently, the muon track's impact point is often inaccurately estimated. This study presents a new algorithm that mitigates the'scattering tail' effect by restoring the original muon track, utilizing a combination of Monte Carlo simulations and machine learning techniques. The algorithm's performance is evaluated through its application to simulated data and is compared to existing methods, demonstrating its ability to significantly reduce the mean square error in the reconstructed muon track.

This research examines the impact of dispersing a nonlinear Schrödinger equation with intensity-based nonlinearity in a periodic, two-dimensional space with a Gaussian noise dispersion pattern, resulting in almost sure local well-posedness for initial conditions within the H^(-1) space.

This research focuses on a specific type of communication system, a multiple access channel with separate wireless connections. In this setup, a sender transmits data through multiple independent channels to a receiver, who needs to decode the message within a specific time frame. The sender and receiver work together to minimize the amount of data sent, while ensuring the message is received within the time limit. The sender can choose from a range of coding methods, including a specific type of error-correcting code, to optimize the transmission. The study investigates how the number of channels affects the performance of the system, particularly when the time frame is limited. The results show that using multiple channels can significantly improve the transmission rate, especially when the time frame is tight. The study also demonstrates that using error-correcting codes can further enhance the performance, especially when the time frame is constrained. The study also explores the impact of the number of channels on the transmission rate, and shows that using more channels can significantly improve the performance. The study also demonstrates that using error-correcting codes can further improve the transmission rate, especially when the number of channels is limited.

The Sgr A East region, a prominent source of X-rays and radio waves near the Milky Way's center, is a complex area of interaction between a stellar explosion and surrounding gas. To understand the origin of Sgr A East, researchers analyzed the motion of the region's gas and dust, and found that the explosion likely occurred within a dense, rotating disk of gas near the center of the Milky Way. This disk, which is approximately 0.06 parsecs in radius, is rotating at a speed of about 10 kilometers per second. By modeling the motion of the region's gas and dust, researchers were able to pinpoint the location of the explosion and found that it occurred within the disk, and that the explosion's energy was released in a relatively short period of time. This research provides new insights into the origin of Sgr A East, and suggests that the region's gas and dust are a result of the interaction between the explosion and surrounding gas.

Recent findings in B-meson decays involving semileptone processes have shown discrepancies with the standard model predictions, particularly in the ratios of muon to electron branching ratios. To address this issue, we have conducted a comprehensive analysis of 10 different B-meson decay processes, examining the distributions of final-state leptons. The results indicate that the observed discrepancies may be attributed to a new, weakly interacting particle that couples with leptons, exhibiting distinct interaction strengths for different lepton flavors. The analysis suggests that the interaction between this particle and charged leptons is more pronounced in muon interactions than in electron interactions, with the magnitude of this difference being consistent with the observed discrepancies in B-meson decays. The analysis also reveals that the interaction between this particle and bottom quarks is relatively weak, with the magnitude of this interaction being consistent with the interaction between this particle and charged leptons. The analysis further suggests that the interaction between this particle and bottom quarks is more pronounced in the case of the B to D* l+ nu l decay process, with the magnitude of this interaction being consistent with the interaction between this particle and charged leptons. The analysis also reveals that the interaction between this particle and bottom quarks is more pronounced in the case of the B to D* l+ nu l decay process, with the magnitude of this interaction being consistent with the interaction between this particle and charged leptons.

This paper outlines a Danish system developed for the 2021 DISRPT2 shared task, focusing on the tasks of segmentation, classification, and identification of connective words. The system's approach combines a sequence labeling model for the first two tasks and a sequence tagging model for the third task. For the latter, our system identifies connective words by utilizing a pre-trained BERT model and fine-tuning it on a small dataset of 100 annotated sentences.

The 6G and beyond wireless networks are expected to be characterized by the coexistence of multiple network operators and infrastructure providers. This will give rise to a new paradigm of network infrastructure sharing, where operators can lease network resources from infrastructure providers. However, this arrangement introduces new challenges, such as ensuring fair resource allocation, incentivizing infrastructure sharing, and maintaining network security. To address these challenges, we propose a novel blockchain-enabled framework for responsible and transparent infrastructure sharing in 6G and beyond. This framework, known as BEAT, incorporates a novel mechanism for incentivizing infrastructure sharing, ensuring fair resource allocation, and maintaining network security. We have evaluated the performance of BEAT through simulations, demonstrating its effectiveness in promoting responsible and transparent infrastructure sharing.

The Okubo-Weiss criterion is a widely used method to identify vortex formation in two-dimensional fluid flows. It relies on a comparison between the vorticity and the difference between the stretching and compressing forces acting on the fluid. This criterion has been successfully applied to a variety of fluid flow scenarios, including barotropic flows, geophysical flows, and magnetized fluids. This study provides a comprehensive mathematical framework for the criterion, which can be used to analyze a broad range of fluid flow scenarios. It also demonstrates that the criterion is rooted in the conservation of potential vorticity and that its applicability is not limited to specific fluid flow scenarios.

Lee-Wick type theories are considered a potential solution to the Standard Model's limitations, yet their effects on the primordial universe's thermodynamics remain largely unexplored. This study examines the thermodynamic properties of a simplified universe model, assuming it consists of non-interacting particles, including Lee-Wick partners. We investigate the behavior of various thermodynamic quantities, such as energy density, pressure, entropy, and heat capacity, as well as the temperature's evolution over time. Our analysis reveals that the entropy and heat capacity exhibit non-monotonic behavior, and we observe that the heat capacity can exhibit negative values. Furthermore, we investigate the conditions under which heat transfer occurs between particles and their partners, and we find that the particles can absorb heat from their partners, resulting in a decrease in the particles' number.

Our approach, StyTr$^2$, is a visual style transfer model based on transformers that enables the visual style of one image to be seamlessly integrated into another image. This method diverges from traditional style transfer techniques by focusing on the visual aspects of style rather than its semantic components. This is achieved through a style-aware transformer that captures the visual style features from the input style image, which are then combined with the input content image to produce the final output. This innovative approach allows for the transfer of visual style attributes such as texture, color, and texture patterns, ultimately resulting in a more aesthetically pleasing and authentic style transfer. Our results demonstrate that StyTr$^2$ produces high-quality visual style transfers that are more visually appealing and faithful to the input style image.

The study of thermodynamic length has garnered significant interest in the field of nonequilibrium thermodynamics, particularly in the context of optimizing work extraction and information processing. However, the practical application of this concept has been hindered by the lack of experimental verification. In this research, we bridge this gap by experimentally demonstrating the optimal properties of Landauer erasure, focusing on the dissipation ratio and thermodynamic length. By utilizing a colloidal particle in a harmonic potential, we establish a direct connection between thermodynamic length and dissipation, and demonstrate that a constant erasure protocol, characterized by a linear relationship with the initial length of the erasure, minimizes the dissipation ratio and maximizes work recovery. Our findings not only validate the principles of Landauer erasure but also provide a framework for optimizing information processing protocols in real-world experiments.

We have investigated the possibility of producing a vector-like T quark at future high-energy electron-positron colliders, considering the theoretical framework of a single vector-like T quark coupled to the Standard Model via contact interactions. Utilizing the cross-section formula for contact interactions, we calculated the minimum energy required to produce the T quark pair at these future colliders, specifically the International Linear Collider and the Compact Linear Collider. The results indicate that these proposed electron-positron colliders could successfully detect the T quark at specific energy levels, namely 3 TeV and 1.5 TeV, respectively.

The stability of a non-equilibrium fluid under acoustic waves is examined, with the fluid's properties described by a specific equation. It is established that a one-dimensional acoustic wave will disperse over time, with the wave's amplitude decreasing at a rate proportional to the inverse of the distance. Additionally, the stability of the wave is proven within a specific, high-energy framework.

This research develops the framework for weighted shifts on generalized directed semi-graphs, encompassing graph shifts and shifts on directed trees as specific instances. The study provides key spectral characteristics and establishes the compact criterion for weighted shifts on generalized directed semi-graphs.

Our research explores the creation of radioactive nuclei and electron-positron pairs through the interaction of an ultra-intense laser with a high-Z target. We've developed a comprehensive model that accounts for the laser's effect on the target and the resulting nuclear reactions. We've also simulated the laser's impact on a high-Z target and found that it can produce significant amounts of radioactive nuclei and electron-positron pairs. Our results show that the creation of radioactive nuclei and electron-positron pairs is primarily due to the laser's interaction with the target, and that it can be used to produce large quantities of these particles. Our findings suggest that an ultra-intense laser could be used as a source of radioactive nuclei and electron-positron pairs, and that it could be used to study the behavior of these particles in extreme conditions.

We introduce Event Identification, a novel task that involves identifying significant and meaningful words in sentences to facilitate event recognition. This task is crucial for developing event representation models that can be used in various applications. To address this challenge, we propose a new approach that leverages the Gate Diversity metric to measure word importance and employs Dependency Graph Convolutional Networks to capture the relationships between words. Our experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in achieving state-of-the-art performance on event classification tasks.

This paper presents a Bayesian framework for addressing error-in-factor regression issues, where unobserved factor scores serve as latent variables in a regression model. A novel Gibbs sampling algorithm is developed to facilitate posterior inference, and its ergodicity is rigorously proven. The proposed method is tested using a combination of Monte Carlo simulations and real-world data analysis.

This study introduces an innovative method for analyzing nonlinear dynamic systems, which incorporates stochastic noise into the analysis. The approach involves solving a complex nonlinear optimization problem to obtain the optimal response of the system, which is formulated as a combination of time-varying coefficients and basis functions. The optimal solution is obtained through the minimization of a cost function that compares the predicted response with the actual system output. The effectiveness of the proposed method is demonstrated using a nonlinear pendulum system, which is subjected to random disturbances.

A model is developed to describe the propagation of waves through a lossy, nonlinear medium, accounting for the effects of reflection, absorption, and nonlinear interaction. The model's parameters are derived from a linear wave equation with a complex damping coefficient, allowing for a clear interpretation of their physical significance. The model's validity is tested against numerical solutions of the full nonlinear wave equation, and a simplified version is derived to facilitate analytical solutions of the nonlinear wave equation.

Reinforcement learning has become a prominent area of research in artificial intelligence, particularly in the context of robotics and robotics-related applications. However, a significant drawback of this approach is its lack of transparency, which hinders its adoption in safety-sensitive and explainable settings. To address this limitation, researchers have developed various methods for enhancing the interpretability of reinforcement learning models. This paper provides a comprehensive review of the existing methods for interpretable reinforcement learning, categorizing them into three main groups: reinforcement learning with pre-trained interpretable models, reinforcement learning with in-built interpretability, and post-hoc reinforcement learning analysis. The review also highlights the current challenges and potential future directions in the field of interpretable reinforcement learning.

In the context of a complete lattice, we are examining logics with a single variable, characterized by their algebraic properties. These logics are defined by their sound and complete axiomatic systems, which are also equivalent to varieties of lattices with specific identities. We are providing an overview of their meaning within an algebraic framework, specifically in the context of the Henkin model. Furthermore, we are establishing a connection between the properties of these logics and those of the Henkin model, which is defined by the properties of the lattice and its associated algebraic properties.

This paper explores the decomposition of a Gaussian process signature into its Wieman chaun components, leveraging this understanding to establish connections between theWieman  chaun  projection  and  the  classical  projection  into  truncated  tensor powers. We derive an explicit Wieman  chaun  decomposition for the signature of a geometric Brownian motion, showcasing its relationship with the Hermite polynomials.

This study examines the performance of MU-MIMO systems in the context of millimeter-wave cellular networks, focusing on the impact of localization errors on network capacity. We develop a novel statistical model to describe the distribution of localization errors in cellular networks, enabling the derivation of the aggregate mutual information across all base stations. We then derive the distribution of mutual information between a specific user and all base stations, as well as the mutual information between a user and the nearest base station. Additionally, we derive the distribution of the signal-to-interference-plus-noise ratio (SINR) for the nearest base station. Our analysis reveals that the mutual information between a user and all base stations is significantly higher than that between the user and the nearest base station, suggesting that multiple base stations can effectively collaborate to enhance user data rates. Our findings are supported by numerical simulations, which validate the accuracy of the proposed statistical models.

We numerically investigate the dynamics of a Bose gas under conditions of low dimensionality and weak inter-particle interactions, focusing on its behavior as it undergoes a phase transition into a Bose-Einstein condensate. Our study reveals that the condensate's behavior is characterized by a non-exponential growth pattern, which is distinct from the critical dynamics observed in three-dimensional systems. Furthermore, we find that the condensate's behavior is governed by a power-law relationship, which is in agreement with theoretical predictions. Our results also demonstrate that the condensate's behavior is influenced by the initial conditions of the system, which is a key factor in understanding its dynamics.

High-definition image restoration is a complex task, requiring the creation of high-quality images from degraded inputs. Existing methods, however, are limited by their reliance on a single-stage process and the use of a single loss function, which restricts their ability to produce high-quality images. To overcome these challenges, a novel two-phase approach is proposed, combining a multi-stage process with a multi-loss function. The approach is further enhanced by the introduction of a multi-scale feature fusion module, which enables the model to capture both local and global image features. The effectiveness of this method is demonstrated through its superior performance on multiple datasets, including Set14, B100, and Urban100.

This research paper delves into the thresholding bandit problem, a complex challenge in the field of multi-armed bandits. The problem involves a multi-armed bandit with an unknown number of positive reward arms, where the goal is to discover all arms with positive rewards within a limited number of iterations. The paper examines the performance of two prominent algorithms, UCB-RT and LUCB, in relation to their respective strengths and weaknesses. The analysis reveals that ULCB's performance is optimal in scenarios with a large number of arms, but its efficiency diminishes in scenarios with a small number of arms. Conversely, a modified version of UCB-RT, dubbed LUCB-RT, exhibits optimal performance in scenarios with a small number of arms, but its efficiency diminishes in scenarios with a large number of arms. The paper also presents a novel algorithm, named LUCB-RT, that combines the strengths of UCB-RT and LUCB to achieve optimal performance in all scenarios. The analysis further demonstrates that LUCB-RT's regret is bounded by $O\left(\frac{\log n}{\Delta^2}\right)$, where $n$ is the total number of arms and $\Delta$ is the minimum gap between the optimal arm's reward and the threshold.

The widespread adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) in various sectors has sparked a range of public reactions, from excitement to apprehension. This study examines the sentiment of people's perceptions towards AI in eight countries, focusing on the emotional responses of English-speaking individuals. By analyzing over 1.2 million social media posts from the United States, United Kingdom, India, Germany, France, Japan, China, and Australia, our research reveals that people's views on AI are highly subjective and vary significantly based on their individual experiences. We discovered that people's views on AI are highly emotional and that certain countries, such as the United States and the United Kingdom, tend to have more positive perceptions, while others like China and Japan tend to have more negative views. This study also highlights the importance of considering cultural and personal factors when developing AI systems that interact with people.

The first measurement of the decay $\Xi_c^0\to\pi^-\Lambda_c^+$ has been achieved, with a branching ratio of $1.1^{+0.6}_{-0.8}$ percent, relative to the decay $\Xi_c^0\to\pi^+\Xi_c^+$. This measurement was made using a dataset of $1.0$ femtobarns collected by the Belle detector at the KEKB collider, where $Z^0$ pairs were produced via $e^+e^-$ collisions at the $\Upsilon(4S)$ resonance.

Reinforcement learning is a crucial area of machine learning with significant applications in robotics, gaming, and autonomous systems. Actor-critic algorithms, a subset of reinforcement learning, have gained prominence due to their ability to efficiently solve complex sequential decision-making problems. Nonetheless, conventional actor-critic algorithms face limitations in handling intricate stochastic environments and achieving optimal policy convergence. To address these challenges, this study introduces an innovative method that leverages the Hamiltonian Monte Carlo technique to enhance actor-critic reinforcement learning. By integrating Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, the proposed approach enables more precise policy gradient estimation and improved policy exploration. Furthermore, this method facilitates the efficient sampling of policy distributions, thereby enhancing the overall performance of the reinforcement learning system. Through a series of simulations, the proposed approach has been shown to outperform traditional actor-critic algorithms in terms of policy convergence and overall performance.

We investigate the behavior of a three-dimensional system composed of three coupled, one-dimensional quantum chains with unequal coupling strengths. This setup leads to the emergence of chiral quantum states, characterized by unequal excitation transfer among the chains. Our analysis reveals that the quantum phase diagram of the Dicke triangle exhibits a complex structure, featuring three distinct regions: two superradiant phases with unique chiral properties and one normal phase. Furthermore, we find that the boundary between the normal and superradiant phases is marked by a tricritical point, where the nature of the phase transition changes from superradiant to non-chiral superradiant. Additionally, we demonstrate that the chirality of the superradiant phases can be controlled by adjusting the coupling strengths of the quantum chains.

In multi-agent reinforcement learning, a key challenge is the credit assignment problem, which involves determining the contribution of each agent to the overall outcome. This issue is particularly pronounced in multi-agent settings where rewards are often shared, making it difficult to accurately assess individual performance. To address this limitation, a new approach called Level-Adaptive Reward Allocation (LARA) is proposed, which assigns rewards based on each agent's learning progress. By leveraging LARA, multi-agent systems can achieve more efficient learning and better coordination, even in complex, large-scale environments. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of LARA in various scenarios, including multi-agent resource allocation and cooperative tasks, where it consistently outperforms existing methods.

This paper presents a novel deep reinforcement learning approach for particle-based robots to navigate and manipulate objects. The proposed method leverages a deep neural network to map sensor inputs to particle movement commands, enabling the robot to navigate towards its target while avoiding obstacles. The approach demonstrates superior performance in object control tasks, outperforming existing methods in both simulation and real-world scenarios. The proposed method's effectiveness is validated through extensive experiments, showcasing its efficiency and scalability in various object manipulation tasks.

The detection of atomic species in exoplanet atmospheres is a crucial aspect of atmospheric characterization, particularly for hot Jupiters. However, some species are challenging to identify due to their low abundance or weak spectral features. The study of potassium, an alkali metal, in exoplanet atmospheres is complicated by the presence of a strong spectral feature from molecular potassium chloride, which can obscure the signal from atomic potassium. In this research, we investigate the potential of combining the spectral features of atomic potassium and molecular potassium chloride to detect potassium in the atmosphere of WASP-31b. Using the CH3D code, we model the transmission spectra of the exoplanet under various scenarios, including the presence of potassium in different abundance levels. Our results show that the signal from atomic potassium can be distinguished from molecular potassium chloride in certain conditions, but the signal is significantly reduced in others. Our findings suggest that the detection of potassium in the atmosphere of WASP-31b is feasible, but the signal is likely to be weak due to the presence of molecular potassium chloride.

High-performance computing (HPC) applications are increasingly being deployed in cloud environments, particularly in HPC-as-a-service (HPCaaS) offerings. However, current HPCaaS solutions primarily rely on volatile memory, resulting in significant performance degradation due to frequent data transfers and checkpointing. To address this issue, we introduce a novel HPCaaS platform that leverages persistent memory, offering a cost-effective solution for HPC applications. Our proposed system, built on Intel's Optane DC Persistent Memory, showcases its potential by enabling efficient data management and high-performance computing tasks. We demonstrate the benefits of persistent memory through a series of experiments, including the acceleration of data-intensive applications and the reduction of checkpointing overhead. Our results indicate that persistent memory can significantly improve the performance of HPC applications, particularly those involving large datasets and frequent checkpointing.

The ability to classify individuals based on their brain activity patterns is a significant goal in neuroscience. Researchers have employed graph-based approaches to model brain activity, but these methods often rely on a single, generic graph template that may not accurately capture the unique characteristics of each individual. To address this limitation, we propose a novel framework that utilizes population-specific information to create personalized brain connectivity graphs for each subject. Our approach involves a contrastive learning-based graph template generation method that generates subject-specific graphs and a graph-based classification model that leverages these customized graphs. We evaluate our method on a widely used dataset, the Human Connectome Project, and demonstrate its effectiveness in achieving superior classification performance compared to existing methods.

This article explores Gauss sums, highlighting their significance in mathematics, including applications to Dirichlet L-functions, the resolution of Fermat's Last Theorem, and the reciprocity laws. Additionally, the text discusses connections between Gauss sums and topological concepts, such as the Poincaré conjecture.

We have observed X-ray Cherenkov radiation in ultra-thin films of beryllium and silicon, which are significantly thinner than previously thought necessary. This discovery is based on the observation of X-ray Cherenkov radiation in beryllium at a thickness of 100 nanometers and in silicon at a thickness of 300 nanometers. The findings are in line with theoretical predictions, which suggest that X-ray Cherenkov radiation can occur in materials at much smaller thicknesses than previously thought. This breakthrough has significant implications for the development of X-ray Cherenkov detectors, which could potentially be miniaturized to unprecedented levels.

A rigorous framework called UCCA has been developed to address the complexities of understanding language. It distinguishes itself from other frameworks by incorporating the concept of pragmatic inference and providing a systematic approach to identifying missing argument information. This paper presents a comprehensive dataset of 1,500 English sentences along with their corresponding implicit argument annotations. The dataset is accompanied by annotated prompts for inference tasks, which can be used to evaluate the performance of language models. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our dataset by showcasing the current state-of-the-art LLMs and their ability to solve UCCA-based tasks, as well as identifying areas for improvement.

In medical imaging, multiple instance learning (MIL) is a technique that allows for the automatic detection of diseases in images without needing detailed labels. However, the current MIL methods have limitations when dealing with complex images and the need for precise disease localization. To address these issues, we have developed a new approach that combines a technique called attention-based MIL with a method of automatically selecting the most important features from the images. This new approach, called autonomous MIL, has been tested on chest X-ray images and has been found to be more accurate than other methods, particularly in identifying diseases and their locations. The results show that the autonomous MIL method outperforms other methods in terms of accuracy and the ability to pinpoint disease locations. The source code for this new approach is available for others to use and build upon.

In the context of limited samples, we investigate the model selection process, focusing on determining the optimal model from a given set of candidates. To achieve this, we introduce a penalized minimization criterion based on the Hellinger divergence, an information-theoretic measure, to quantify the discrepancy between the true data distribution and the candidate models. This approach is motivated by the need to overcome the limitations of existing methods, such as the Kullback-Leibler divergence, which may not be well-suited for finite samples. We establish the theoretical foundation of our proposed criterion, including its consistency and accuracy in terms of model equivalence, and demonstrate its performance through simulations and a real-world application involving the analysis of gene expression data.

Our research focuses on binary sequences and their associated motifs, particularly exploring the Prouhet-Thue-Morse sequence, which is a key sequence in this area. We have developed a comprehensive analysis of the occurrence of every binary motif in the Prouhet-Thue-Morse sequence, a sequence that exhibits self-similarity. This self-similarity is a result of the sequence being generated through a recursive process. We have also discovered that certain binary motifs do not occur in the sequence, and we have provided a complete classification of these non-occurring motifs. Furthermore, we have established a recursive formula for the number of occurrences of a given binary motif in the first n terms of the Prouhet-Thue-Morse sequence, which is a key contribution of this work.

In the realm of machine learning, dynamic classifier selection has been extensively researched, with the aim of enhancing overall performance by leveraging the strengths of multiple base classifiers. However, existing methods often overlook the nuanced relationship between the cost of prediction and the specific task at hand. To address this limitation, we introduce a price-sensitive hierarchical grouping approach that considers the varying costs of different tasks. By grouping base classifiers hierarchically and selecting the optimal classifier based on the cost-benefit ratio, our method achieves superior performance compared to existing techniques, as demonstrated through our experiments on two benchmark datasets.

The Tianlai project, a large-scale radio telescope array, is being developed in China to create a global network of low-frequency radio arrays. This project aims to study the early universe, including the cosmic dawn and reionization periods, and will also contribute to research on pulsars and other celestial phenomena. The Tianlai experiment, which will operate at frequencies between 30 and 300 MHz, will utilize an array of 1000 telescopes, each with a 10-meter diameter. The project's information processing pipeline is designed to handle the large amount of data generated by the array, including data collection, calibration, and analysis. This pipeline will enable researchers to study various phenomena, including the cosmic microwave background, the early universe, and pulsars, and will also provide a platform for future research in radio astronomy.

Additionally, we discovered that these materials possess a high Curie temperature, with values of 1000 K, 100 K, and 100 K, respectively. Our findings suggest that these materials could be used as potential spintronic materials.

The attributable fraction among the exposed (AFE) is a vital measure in epidemiology, quantifying the proportion of adverse outcomes in an exposed group that can be attributed to a specific risk factor. Traditionally, AFE is calculated using population-level data, but this method may be inadequate when the risk factor is complex or difficult to measure. In this study, we demonstrate how case narrative data can be leveraged to calculate AFE, utilizing a case-control study on intimate partner violence (IPV) and its impact on the development of depression among women. We develop a machine learning model to classify women's exposure to IPV based on their depression narratives, and apply this model to estimate AFE. The results show that AFE calculated from case narratives is comparable to those from traditional methods, and highlight the potential of using case narratives to assess the effects of hard-to-measure risk factors.

If $X$ has $k$-rational points, then $\zeta$ is linearly equivalent to a rational point, provided that $k$ is either an infinite field with characteristic $0$, a perfect field with characteristic $p\geq \text{char}(K)-d+2$, or a non-perfect field with characteristic $-\infty$ with $X(k)$ being dense in its reduced scheme.

The production of $\Upsilon$(2S) and $\Upsilon$(3S) mesons in proton-proton collisions at 7 TeV was studied using data from the LHC, collected by the ALICE detector. Measured in transverse momentum and rapidity intervals, the ratios of $\Upsilon$(nS) cross-sections were determined. These ratios were found to be consistent with each other within uncertainties, and the ALICE data agreed with existing measurements from other experiments. The study also compared the $\Upsilon$(3S) to $\Upsilon$(2S) and $\Upsilon$(2S) to $\Upsilon$(1S) ratios with predictions from various models, including color-singlet and color-octet models, and found that the latter is more consistent with the ALICE data.

The global Torelli conjecture for Teichmüller spaces is explored in relation to projective varieties. Its validity is demonstrated for abelian varieties, torus bundles, and specific cases, such as products of abelian varieties and curves of genus 2. Additionally, the conjecture is supported for curves with at most three singularities and for certain projective varieties, like products of abelian varieties and curves of genus 2. The conjecture is also proven for a broader class of projective varieties, encompassing products of abelian varieties and curves of genus 2.

We introduce a novel method for creating a personalized, neural-based digital representation of an individual from a single video clip. This representation, called an implicit neural avatar, is a neural network that maps 3D spatial coordinates to surface features, such as color and texture. We propose a new training approach that leverages a pre-trained model of the human body to guide avatar learning, ensuring realistic body shapes. This approach combines a novel loss function that enforces the avatar to adhere to the human body model, while also incorporating video data to capture surface appearance. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method by showcasing its ability to generate high-quality, photorealistic digital avatars from a single video clip, and our results outperform existing methods in terms of accuracy and realism.

This paper presents a novel face inpainting technique that utilizes a Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) to generate missing facial regions. The approach involves three main stages: (1) decomposing a face image into texture and geometry using a 3D Morphable Model (3DMM); (2) inpainting the face's geometry and texture separately, with the GAN trained on diverse facial geometries to fill gaps; (3) reconstructing the face image from the completed 3DMM parameters. The proposed method was tested on various datasets, including images with occlusions, and achieved promising results.
This paper provides a brief overview of Intrinsically-Driven Reinforcement Learning, presenting relevant equations and algorithms for key methods, and highlighting their distinct characteristics.

This paper introduces a novel, localized strategy iteration algorithm for multi-agent reinforcement learning, which utilizes only information from a limited neighborhood. The algorithm is founded on a concept of localized optimal value functions, which are defined for each agent in conjunction with the actions of its neighboring agents. A localized strategy iteration process is then defined, which updates each agent's value function and policy based on the actions of its neighbors. The convergence of this localized strategy iteration process is proven, and the conditions for its convergence to the global optimum are established. Furthermore, a distributed implementation of this algorithm is presented, which enables each agent to independently compute its own optimal value function and policy. The distributed algorithm is evaluated through experiments on a grid world environment, demonstrating its convergence to the global optimum.

A study of specific jet patterns in high-energy proton collisions is presented, focusing on events with a notable gap in the rapidity region between the leading jets. The analysis is based on a dataset of 5.1 fb^-1 of data collected at 7 TeV by the CMS detector at the LHC. The observed gap in rapidity is found to be substantial, with a median value of 1.8 and a notable fraction of 10% of events exhibiting such a gap. The study investigates the relationship between the gap in rapidity and the transverse momentum of the leading jet, as well as the angular separation between the jets. The analysis also examines the distribution of jet pseudorapidity and reports on the dijet mass and transverse momentum distributions.

Silicon's potential to serve as a versatile material has been well-documented, and researchers are now exploring its potential in the field of thermoelectric applications. A recent study has identified a previously overlooked thermoelectric material, penta-silicene, a two-dimensional material with a pentagonal structure. The researchers utilized the density functional theory to investigate the electronic and thermal properties of penta-silene, and their findings revealed that it possesses a high thermoelectric figure of merit, ZT, at room temperature, with values of 1.1 and 1.2 for the armchair and zigzag edges, respectively. The researchers also discovered that doping penta-silene with hydrogen and fluorine can significantly enhance its thermoelectric performance, with ZT values of 1.3 and 1.4, respectively. The results of this study have significant implications for the development of thermoelectric applications, and penta-silene is poised to become a leading candidate for the next generation of thermoelectric materials.

In this study, we investigate the impact of a magnetized-hot medium on quarkonia properties within a fractional non-relativistic quark model. We consider a potential consisting of a Cornell potential, a deconfinement term, a color-magnetic interaction, and a spin-spin interaction, and introduce a thermal correction to the gluon propagator. We analyze the dissociation temperatures of quarkonia states in a QCD medium with a magnetic field, and our results show that the dissociation temperatures are higher in the presence of a magnetic field. We also study the effect of a magnetic field on the spectral properties of quarkonia states, and our findings indicate that the magnetic field causes a redshift in the spectral lines.

We investigate the interaction of dark matter with the Earth's atmosphere, space, and ancient rocks, and how this interaction can be detected through the scattering of dark matter particles. Focusing on the scattering of dark matter on neutron stars, cosmic rays, and old rocks, we examine the sensitivity of these interactions to the mass of dark matter and its coupling to fermions. Our analysis reveals that dark matter with masses between 100 GeV and 1 TeV can be detected through the scattering of dark matter on neutron stars, cosmic rays, and ancient rocks, and that the sensitivity of these interactions is comparable to that of direct detection experiments.

We have developed a novel reinforcement learning algorithm that tackles a complex game called SIGG with uncertain information. This game involves a sender and a receiver, where the sender has private knowledge of the game's state. The receiver can either act based on the sender's message or request additional information. The receiver's decision is influenced by the sender's private knowledge, and the sender's utility is influenced by the receiver's additional information request. The proposed algorithm, SIGG-RL, learns the optimal strategy for both the sender and receiver through self-play. The sender's strategy involves sending messages that maximize the sender's utility, and the receiver's strategy involves asking for additional information when it is beneficial. The proposed algorithm is shown to be effective in finding a stable equilibrium in the game.

Robots operating in unpredictable environments, such as those with non-uniform terrain, are prone to plan failures due to model inaccuracies. To address this issue, we've developed a novel framework, called TERP, that integrates planning and control to ensure reliable robot navigation. TERP leverages a deep reinforcement learning approach to create a robust planner that can adapt to model uncertainties and prevent failures. By incorporating a probabilistic model of the environment, TERP enables the robot to assess the likelihood of planning failures and make informed decisions to avoid them. Our framework's effectiveness is demonstrated through successful experiments on a real-world outdoor terrain with uneven ground.

The behavior of a three-dimensional model with a long-range Kac potential is investigated, which exhibits phase separation at low temperatures. A phase diagram is constructed, detailing the relationship between phase separation and model parameters. This diagram is analyzed through a variational approach, utilizing a trial density profile to calculate the free energy of the system. This free energy is then used to determine the critical line separating the dipolar and macroscopic phases, as well as the first-order transition line separating the dipolar and mixed phases.

This study focuses on a two-dimensional inverse problem for a conductivity inclusion. The problem involves determining the conductivity distribution within a bounded region, known as the inclusion, based on boundary measurements obtained from an electric potential model. The problem is formulated as a minimization task, where the objective function comprises a data mismatch term and a regularization term. The data mismatch term is defined by the squared L2 norm of the difference between the measured data and model prediction, while the regularization term is a total variation penalty. The problem is solved using a gradient-based method, where the gradient of the objective function is computed using an adjoint state approach. The method is tested using numerical experiments on a two-dimensional domain with a circular inclusion. The results show that the method is effective in recovering the true conductivity distribution, even in the presence of noisy data. The study also investigates the effect of the regularization parameter on the solution quality, finding that the optimal value depends on the noise level in the data. The study concludes that the proposed method is effective in solving the inverse problem for a planar conductivity inclusion.

We investigate the conditions under which a star's magnetic field remains stable,
balancing magnetic forces with centrifugal forces and gravity. Our analysis
reveals that a toroidal magnetic field can be unstable in the presence of rotation,
but remains stable in the absence of radial movement. In contrast, a poloidal
magnetic field is generally stable, except in cases where the magnetic forces
dominate over centrifugal forces. The implications of our findings on the
evolution of stars and their magnetic fields are also explored.

We introduce a concept called simplicial coordination, which is a measure of how a simplicial complex is embedded in a graph. This concept is defined as the minimum number of vertices needed to represent the complex in a graph through simplicial coordination. We investigate the relationship between simplicial coordination and other graph parameters, such as clique number and chromatic number, and establish connections to topological concepts like the clique number and chromatic number of the graph. We also show that simplicial coordination is closely related to the simplicial dimension of the graph, and we provide a formula for calculating the simplicial dimension of a graph. Additionally, we investigate the relationship between simplicial coordination and the clique number of a graph, and we provide a formula for calculating the clique number of a graph in terms of simplicial coordination. We also study the simplicial coordination of a graph in terms of its chromatic number, and we provide a formula for calculating the simplicial coordination of a graph in terms of its chromatic number.

Sparse matrix operations are fundamental components in many computational workflows, particularly in linear algebra and graph processing. Optimizing the performance of these operations is crucial for achieving faster execution times. This study explores optimization techniques for the sparse matrix-vector multiplication (SpMV) operation, which is a key building block for linear systems algorithms. We examine the performance of the CSR and SKS storage formats on the GPU, focusing on the CUDA framework. We analyze the impact of various optimization methods, such as data layout transformations, on SpMV performance, and evaluate their effectiveness in iterative linear algorithms, including the Conjugate Gradient (CG) method.

The problem of sharing a finite set of values among functions $f$ and $g$ in an open subset of the complex plane is investigated, with the functions agreeing on these values and their derivatives, leading to the conclusion that $f$ and $g$ are identical. This problem is addressed for a broad class of functions, including entire, meromorphic, and specific types of functions, with a particular focus on entire functions of a certain growth and meromorphic functions of a certain rank.

The widespread use of AR technology in everyday life is anticipated to increase, with mobile AR devices becoming a common tool for enhancing user experiences.  A significant challenge lies in the need for users to effectively communicate their intentions to the AR system, which is often complicated by the limitations of hands-free input methods.  To address this issue, we introduce the HAIR system, which is designed to enhance hands-free AR interactions by incorporating head-mounted displays and a head-purpose recognition module.  Our research demonstrates the effectiveness of HAIR in improving the efficiency of hands-free interactions, as evidenced by a user study that compared its performance against a traditional mobile AR system.  The results show that HAIR significantly reduces interaction time and enhances user satisfaction, indicating its potential as a valuable tool for facilitating hands-free AR interactions.

The growth and detachment of bubbles from electrodes during electrolysis is significantly affected by the surrounding fluid dynamics. In environments with minimal movement, the bubble growth rate is primarily influenced by the diffusion of ions, whereas in environments with minimal fluid movement, the bubble growth rate is determined by the diffusion of ions. However, when the fluid is driven by natural convection, the diffusion layer is disrupted, leading to a significant increase in the bubble growth rate. This phenomenon has been observed in experiments involving aluminum anodes in a 0.1 M NaOH solution, where the diffusion layer is periodically removed, allowing for the growth of larger bubbles. This effect has been observed in both single and multiple bubble scenarios, and it has been shown that the growth rate of bubbles is significantly increased when the diffusion layer is disrupted. This phenomenon has significant implications for the design of gas diffusion electrodes, and it highlights the importance of considering the fluid dynamics in the development of such devices.

A thorough examination of the possibility of the existence of long-lived particles, specifically a hypothetical scalar boson that decays into a photon, is conducted using data from proton-proton collisions at 13 TeV. The analysis is based on 139 fb$^{-1}$ of collected data by the CMS detector. The investigation focuses on scenarios where a photon is emitted and detected, and where the photon's energy is above 5 GeV. The analysis is conducted in relation to the scalar boson's mass, which ranges from 5 GeV to 100 GeV, and its lifetime, which ranges from 10$^{-10}$ to 10$^{-2}$ seconds. The results of this study are reported in terms of 95% confidence level exclusion limits on the coupling between the scalar boson and photons.

In the context of two-dimensional Dirac semimetals, researchers have discovered a phenomenon where a second-order topological phase can be achieved through the application of spin-orbit coupling and an external magnetic field. This discovery is significant as it provides a way to create a second-order topological phase in materials that are inherently non-magnetic. However, a recent study has revealed that a similar phenomenon can also be achieved in materials that are non-magnetic, provided that the spin-orbit coupling is accompanied by the Coulomb interaction. This discovery is based on a theoretical model that incorporates a specific type of spin-orbit coupling, which is capable of inducing a second-order topological phase in materials that are non-magnetic. The model also takes into account the Coulomb interaction, which is a key factor in the emergence of this phenomenon. The results of this study have important implications for the development of new materials that can be used in a wide range of applications, including the development of new types of electronic devices.

This paper introduces a novel approach for developing concurrent programs from sequential code, leveraging Answer Set Programming to automate the process. The method involves defining a set of answerable queries that capture data access patterns, which are then used to generate a conflict graph. This graph is transformed into concurrent code using a rule-based system, ensuring data race freedom and adherence to sequential semantics. The approach is demonstrated through a case study, showcasing its effectiveness in creating optimized concurrent programs from sequential algorithms.

A new approach to testing theories of gravity that go beyond the general theory, is presented. This involves using a magnetically suspended device to measure the gravitational force between masses with different compositions. This method is particularly useful for testing theories that propose the existence of new forces, which could be related to the dark matter. This technique is also suitable for experiments conducted in space, where it can be used to study the gravitational behavior of masses in microgravity.

We've identified two new variants of ethynyl cyclopentadiene in the TMC-1 molecular cloud, specifically 1,5-dihydro-1-ethynyl cyclopenta-1,3-diene and 1,5-dihydro-1-methyl-1-ethynyl cyclopenta-1,3-diene. These newly detected species were discovered through the analysis of their distinct spectral patterns in the 3.0-3.2 mm range. We've also detected two other variants of cyclopentadiene, 1,3-cyclopentadiene and 1,5-dihydro-1-methynyl cyclopentadiene, in the same cloud. These findings have allowed us to determine the column densities of these species, which are 1.1 x 10^12 cm^-2, 1.1 x 10^11 cm^-2, 1.0 x 10^11 cm^-2, and 1.0 x 10^10 cm^-2, respectively. These abundances of these species are comparable to those of CCH and CN, which suggests that the formation of these species is likely to occur through a similar mechanism. This finding has implications for the understanding of the formation of aromatic and aliphatic rings in interstellar space.
